chapter_theme: First songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 1 of 6): the poet renounces women, sects, patron-poetry and birth, vows not to forget the word and the feet given him at Arunai, sees each charm of a woman as Death's weapon, and pictures the funeral and Yama's noose; three songs are laments of a lovesick girl tormented by the moon, the flute and the town's talk. The praise dwells on Arunai's tall tower, Murugan as teacher of Siva, and his love for Valli.
structure_note: Renunciation and longing for silence (368, 370), the quarrelling sects (369), the word and feet given at Arunai (371, 373), women's charms seen as their dangers (372, 374), courtesans who sell (373, 375, 377), death and Yama's noose (376, 378), the akam laments (379 to 381), and 382, which asks to be taken into service before death. 376 to 381 name the tower (கோபுரம்) of Arunai.

368.reading: The poet says 'enough, enough' (அலம் அலம்) to lovemaking with women, to the learning that likens men of the world to the wish-tree, to form and youth, to the arts of perverse sects, to the bewildering life of deeds and to births like writing on water, and asks now for his feet and for silence, to walk one way with his devotees. The praise tells at length of Siva's burning of the three cities, the chariot breaking under his foot and the cities blazing at his laugh, and names Murugan his son, who melted with the hunter girl and roams on a peacock over the peak of Arunai with its seven-tiered towers.
368.nuance: The refrain அலமலம் sweeps away not only women but the poet's own trade: உலகோரைத் தருவை நிகரிடு புலமை is the art of praising patrons as the kalpa tree. சலில லிபியன சனனம், births like letters written on water, is a striking image of impermanence. The Tripura story is told in its full details (Meru as bow, the serpent king as string, sun and moon as wheels, Brahma as charioteer, the Vedas as horses), and the three spared devotees appear as ஒருவரும் இருவரும் அருள்பெற.

369.reading: The poet sets against the pitiless, hair-plucked night-wanderers, flesh-eaters and many quarrelsome sectarians who wail broken scriptures till the path is lost, the reality without rising or death which the Vedas drum is easily gained in knowledge when the eyes stream, the words falter, the heart melts, craving, worldly bonds, speech, act and feeling end, the two deeds fall away and 'mine' is shaken off; he asks when that day of grace will come. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess, Gauri, Bhairavi, Tripurai, the faithful wife who bore all worlds, and names Murugan her son and Ganga's, the guru brighter than countless suns, who gave the forest girl and the gods' daughter their place beside him at Arunai.
369.nuance: பறிதலை நிசிசரர், the hair-plucked night-wanderers, likely means Jain monks, who pluck their hair; பிசித அசனர், flesh-eaters, may be another group. The conditions are stacked as a chain of 'if' clauses (விடில், கெடில், அறில்) ending in எனது எனும் மலம் அறில், 'if the impurity called mine ends'. The Goddess's names in the praise are partly Sanskrit compounds whose divisions are uncertain.

370.reading: The poet pictures the women without bounds who sell their sweet lovemaking at a price in every street, their hair and garments loosening, breasts swaying, eyes speaking Kama's scripture, so that men, gods and sages run after them, and asks when his life, tossing in the sea of pleasure they give, will plunge instead into the sea of silent Siva-bliss. The praise paints Arunai, its areca palms tearing the sky so that clouds, moon and the sun's horses stumble, its fields, tanks, moat and walls, and the hill stream carrying agil, flowers, gems, goats, elephants and lions, where Murugan bowed melting at the feet of the hunter girl born of a sage.
370.nuance: The song is built on two seas: the சுக சலதி the women give and the மவுன சிவசுக சலதி the poet longs for. வரைவில் அரிவையர் and விலைகூறும் use the very terms of the Kural's chapter on women who draw no line. முநி தரு புனிதை, the pure one born of a sage, points to the story of Valli's birth.

371.reading: The poet says that even if he melts at women's eyes, hair, smile, lips, waist, gait and feet, speaks their names, runs their errands, strays from the path, jests with them and loses himself in the sea of passion on their bed, he will not forget the one supreme word and the two feet that Murugan gave him with compassion at Arunai. The praise shows the vel trampling the seven hills, breaking Meru's peak and tearing the old mango tree in the sea, names Murugan Siva's son and Ganapati's brother, and has him, for the hunters' salvation, write a lone madal out of longing for the doe of the millet field.
371.nuance: அருணை நகர்மிசை கருணையொடு அருளிய பரம ஒரு வசனமும் இரு சரணமும் மறவேனே: the poet speaks of a word and the feet given to him at Arunai, apparently his own initiation; the vow is not to be pure but not to forget, even in the midst of desire. தனி மடல் எழுதிய makes Murugan the lover who takes the desperate madal for Valli. முதுசூதம், the old mango, is Sura in tree form.

372.reading: The poet asks not to spend day and night praising women in set comparisons, hair as darkness that fights the clouds, face as the moon, eyes as arrows, breasts as lotus buds, nor to flatter them that their form is beauty, but to be told by grace to think daily of Murugan's procession on the peacock that crushes the asuras. The praise has Murugan, amid sages, tell the hidden meaning called hard to speak to Siva who burned the cities with a laugh, and has poets, scholars and ascetics declare him the six-faced one who drank from the six mothers, while devotees dance and worship at Arunai.
372.nuance: The fault confessed is poetic: the set similes of love poetry spent on women, against which the poet sets a new subject, the peacock procession (பவனி). புகல அரியது பொருள் இது ... புதை பொருள் விரகொடு புகல்வோனே is the teaching of Siva, though Om is not named. Two glyphs in the first lines are garbled.

373.reading: The poet lists the courtesans who weigh a man's capital and life, scent themselves with civet and agil, throw spear-like glances, measure the heart by the money and keep their word an instant, and says that he, deluded on their path and knowing neither the foot nor the crown, will not forget the silent word and the two great feet given with compassion at Arunai. The praise tells of Rama against Ravana's walled city, Hanuman's fire and the monkeys' causeway, names Murugan his nephew, and the vel that broke the asuras and restored the gods, and his embrace of the hunter girl.
373.nuance: மனது திரவியம் அளவளவு அளவியர், women who measure their heart exactly to the money, is the stock charge against courtesans. அடிமுடி அறிகிலன், 'I who know neither foot nor crown', may glance at Arunai's own story of the Lord whose foot and crown Vishnu and Brahma could not find, though the song does not tell it. The refrain repeats 371 with மவுன வசனம், the word of silence.

374.reading: The poet takes each charm of women and names what it truly is: the eyes not lotuses but fire-dipped arrows, the hair not a cloud but a darkness that blinds the eye of jnana, the speech not nectar but a net for life, the smile not jasmine but theft, the navel not a pool but a pit, the breasts not hills but Yama the killer, the pearls on them Yama's rope; women are not women but forms made of many deeds, and he asks when he will join with that awareness. The praise shows Valli and Devayanai at his sides, the asura armies burned, and Murugan son of compassionate Uma who fosters dharma, at Arunai where the pure sage Gautama worships.
374.nuance: Each line turns on அல, 'not': the poet undoes the love poet's similes (as 372 renounces them) and replaces each with a danger. மகளிர் மகளிரும் அல பல வினைகொடு சமையும் உருவு: the conclusion is metaphysical, that the woman is a body built of karma. கவுதம புநித முநி தொழ and அறம் வளர் கருணை உமை may point to a local story of Uma's penance at Arunai under the sage Gautama, which the song does not tell.

375.reading: The poet pictures women who walk the street like peacocks, smeared with musk, showing their breasts for sale, their hair falling and garments loose, and calls himself the fool who embraces their delusion, tasting their lips as cane and fruit; he asks for grace that scatters his base and murderous sins. The praise makes the drums sound 'Kumara Gurupara' six times over as their beat while gods, sages and Brahma worship, and names the vel that broke the asuras' horses, elephants and chariots and Murugan who embraced the hunter girl of the red hill.
375.nuance: விலைமுலை, breasts for sale, names the trade. குமர குருபர repeated six times is given as the drums' own rhythm (எனதாளம் குரைசெய் முரசம்), so the name of the Lord becomes the beat. ஒரு அருண கிரி குறமகள் plays on Arunagiri, the red hill, which is also the poet's name. One word (இத்ழுறல், probably இதழூறல்) is garbled.

376.reading: The poet pictures his death: his wife wailing 'you have undone me, husband, I am ruined', his sons crying 'father', kin and old friends weeping round the bier, drums beating, and Yama casting his thick noose; at that hour he asks Murugan to protect him and give back his life. The praise names Murugan with vel, cock and peacock dwelling in the tower of Arunai, lord of the gods, easy for poets of rare Saiva song, lover of the hunter girl on the golden hill, and the warrior who crushed Sura with mountain and sea.
376.nuance: The wailing is given in direct speech (கயல்விழித் தேன் எனைச் செயல் அழித்தாய், கணவ கெட்டேன், புதல்வர் அப்பா). பரிகரித்து ஆவியைத் தரவேணும் asks not for release but for the life itself to be saved at the noose. அருணையிற் கோபுரத்து உறைவோனே, the Murugan of the tower, recurs in 377 and 378.

377.reading: The poet speaks of women whose carp-eyes dance like Death who stirs the life, who settle the body's terms in advance, make relations in secret for coin, cause grief and sulk on the flower bed and give themselves for a high price, and says that for this painful deed he has lost his mind's sense; he asks whether he will worship the two feet that are the raft for life. The praise names Brahma who recites the Vedas, Indra with the vajra and Siva who comes with Uma, the vel that fought Sura so that the peaks and the sea dried, Murugan of the tower at Arunai sung by the wise, and the warrior who longed for the forest girl.
377.nuance: காசினுக்கு உறவு, relation for coin, and உயர் பொருட்கு, for a high price, name the trade. உயிர்ப் புணை இணைத் தாள், the feet as a raft for the life, is an image of crossing. The opening lines (கறுவுமிக் காவியைக் கலகும் அக் காலன் ஒத்து) and முற்பாடு கட்டளை are hard to divide, and the praise's மறைகள் புக்கார் is unclear.

378.reading: The poet imagines Death casting his thick noose, the life going out, the kin of passion no longer holding on, and the body left to the fire and its remains to the water; he, a dog born in this sinful birth and wasted by disease, asks whether he will hear Murugan say with love 'I have forgiven your fault, I have cut away your flaw'. The praise is obscure; it seems to name Murugan the god of the red cock banner who pierced the hill and expounded the arts, and closes as 377 does, at the tower of Arunai.
378.nuance: பிழை பொறுத்தாய் எனப் பழுது அறுத்தாள் என: the grace asked for is forgiveness spoken aloud. The first line repeats 376's பரியகைப் பாசம் விட்டு எறியும் காலன. The praise lines 9 to 13 (கரியமெய்க் கோலமுற்ற அரியின் ...) are hard to divide, and the last two lines are identical to 377's.

379.reading: In the voice of a lovesick woman: by the moonlight that strikes her bed of fire, by the arrows of the fierce god of love who attacked without knowing her state, and by the blame the women of the town speak, her life is all but gone, and she asks Murugan to come daily on his peacock so that it does not perish. The praise names him the bridegroom of the hunter girl, the hero whose feet Siva cherished like flowers on his serpent-wreathed hair, dwelling in the tower of Arunai, who uprooted the asuras and freed the gods.
379.nuance: This is akam poetry in the woman's own voice (எனது ஆவி), the poet in the role of the girl in love with the god. The classical torments are here, the moon and Kama's arrows, with the town's gossip (வருண மட மாதர் கற்ற வசை). The line on Siva placing flowers on his hair (சடிலமுடி மீது வைத்த கடிய மலர் ஆதரித்த கழல்) may mean that Siva wears Murugan's feet; the division is uncertain.

380.reading: Again in the lovesick woman's voice: so that she does not perish from the full moon born of the submarine fire, from the blame of foolish women, from the sweet lone flute and from old King Kama, she asks Murugan to come daily on his blue peacock, so she may know how to embrace his twelve shoulders garlanded with kadamba and kura. The praise names Arunai's tower and tanks, the chest that never leaves the hunter girl, the guru who taught Siva from the first, and the deliverer of Brahma, Vishnu and the gods from prison.
380.nuance: The torments now include the flute (வேயிசை), a classical herald of evening longing. The moon born of the வடவாமுகம், the submarine mare-fire, explains why its light burns. சிவனை முதல் ஓதுவித்த குருநாதா: முதல் may be the first syllable, Om.

381.reading: Told of a girl rather than by her: so that the full infatuation of the woman with breasts like Meru may end, harried by the moon that rises after plunging through the submarine fire, by the yazh sweet as speech, by the sea wailing round the eight directions, and by the formless Kama's arrows, Murugan is asked to come on his emerald peacock. The praise names Rama, who cut Ravana's twenty arms and ten crowns, as his uncle, and Murugan the guru who made Siva study the silent Veda, dwelling in the tower of fierce Arunagiri, whose vel pierced the hill and the eight serpents.
381.nuance: The speaker is now a third person (a mother or friend), as in 24. மவுன மறை ஓதுவித்த, taught the silent Veda, links the teaching of Siva with the silence asked for in 368 and 370. One word (வடவையன லு஡டு) has a corrupt glyph.

382.reading: The poet, infatuated by eyes like poison, lips, hair, smile, brow, gait and breasts, sunk in the misery of Death's trident and tightening noose, asks whether, before he dies with his old deeds unshed, Murugan will not take him into his service. The praise names him the light, Muruga, eternal, who took the hunter girl on his shoulder, Kandavel of the street of the ancient jnana-hill Sonagiri, son of the one who shares Uma, and the comrade-lord of those who sing scattering flowers of knowledge on his feet.
382.nuance: ஏவல் கொண்டிடாயோ, 'will you not take my service', asks to become a servant before death. பழய ஞானச் சோணகிரி calls the red hill itself a hill of ancient knowledge. பாடுமவர் தோழத் தம்பிரானே, lord who is comrade to his singers, may echo the Saiva title of Sundarar, the Lord's comrade, from the other side. The last two lines are identical to 383's.

links.note: Both see the sects as people wandering off, each crying its own 'this is supreme'. Tirumular's remedy is to go the ordained way and seek the King; 369's is to melt in devotion and drop 'mine', when the reality the Vedas proclaim is easily gained.

Both use the Kural's word for courtesans (வரைவிலா, வரைவில்) and picture their pleasure as something a man sinks into: the Kural's mire (அளறு), 370's sea of pleasure, which 370 sets against a second sea, the bliss of Siva.
Both make the courtesan a woman who weighs: in the Kural she weighs the profit and speaks of her virtue to match, in 373 she measures her heart to the money (திரவியம் அளவளவு அளவியர்).

Both end the plea with the same vow, not to forget the word and the two feet given at Arunai; 371 confesses every pleasure first, 373 every deceit of the women, and both keep the vow inside the confession.

The Kural's lover discovers that Death has a woman's eyes, half in wonder; 374 extends the discovery to every charm, breasts as Yama and the pearls on them as Yama's rope, and turns it into a reason to turn away.
Both open the hour of death with the same formula, Yama casting his thick-handed noose (பரியகைப் பாசம் விட்டு எறியும்); 376 asks for the life to be saved, 378 for the fault to be forgiven.
Both count the flute among the torments of the lovesick woman: the Kural's herdsman's flute is a weapon that kills, and 380's sweet lone flute is one of four things she asks to survive.

source_issues: Song 372: unflagged garble யென்முவா (line 3), probably என மூவா.
Song 375: unflagged garble ளித்ழுறல் (line 9), probably இதழூறல். In this chapter the source seems to write ்மு and ்ழு where மூ and ழூ are meant (also துன்ப்முழ்கி in 382).
Song 381: one corrupt character in லு஡டு (line 1), clearly ஊடு.

Song 382: unflagged garble துன்ப்முழ்கித் (line 6), probably துன்பமூழ்கி. Its last two lines (பாதமலர் மீதிற் போதமலர் தூவிப் பாடுமவர் தோழத் தம்பிரானே) are identical to song 383's; one may have been copied into the other.
Songs 377 and 378: the last two lines are identical (அடவியிற் றோகைபொற் றடமுலைக் காசையுற் றயருமச் சேவகப் பெருமாளே); possibly a copying error.
